1:
The invitation to a ruler’s table is read as a danger before an honour. Charles Ellicott corrects the received rendering: the reader is told to consider not what is before him but who, since the host is no equal but one who if offended might do him deadly harm, and the dainties are deceitful because not offered out of friendship, an unguarded word in the insecurity of the festive hour being enough to ruin a guest. Keil and Delitzsch read it the same way, that the man before you is not your equal but one higher, who can destroy you as well as serve you; they render the second line as a warning to the man of good appetite, and dispute the grammar with scholars who make it a statement rather than a command, answering that the tense continues the exhortation and that their reading would have required another word order. Matthew Henry treats the whole as a lesson in entering temptation: the guest sees such a table as he has seldom seen and thinks only of the honour done him, forgetting the snare; the temptation may be stronger to a man not used to such entertainments than to one who always sits down to a good table, and a wise host will take it as an affront for a guest to disorder himself at his table.

Adam Clarke gives the practical version: eat moderately when invited to the table of your betters, do not appear as if half starved at home, and do not eat unaccustomed delicacies, which please without profiting and are injurious to health. He calls these prudential cautions to be observed by anyone who would avoid the conduct of a clown. John Gill offers three senses for the knife at the throat, a restraint on too much talk, where men grow free after eating and say things that give offence; a mortifying of the appetite, like cutting off a right hand; or a reminder to the guest that he sits in danger, and that to be free with the food or drink would be as good as cutting his own throat. John Wesley keeps the last of these, and Gill adds that the dainties may be lawfully desired but not sinfully lusted after.

The warning against labouring to be rich is handled as a companion to the first. Henry says plainly that as some are given to appetite so others are given to covetousness, and that men cheat themselves as much by setting their hearts on money as on dainties; those who aim at great things fill their hands with more business than they can grasp, so that their life is a perfect drudgery and a perpetual hurry, and he counsels a man to be master of what he has rather than its slave. Clarke turns to the maxim of the world, which he gives in a Latin line to the effect that a man should get a fortune honestly if he can, but if not, get one at all events; that, he says, is the devil’s counsel, and well it is followed. He adds that a man who does get wealth must not forget the poor, or the curse of God will be a canker in his gold. Gill takes the labour forbidden to be the over-anxious kind, carried to weariness and to gaping for breath. On the wisdom to be ceased from, Ellicott glosses it as the cleverness shown in piling up wealth and Wesley as the worldly wisdom that persuades men to use all possible means of getting riches; and on the riches that take wing Ellicott would render the line as an eagle flying toward heaven, far beyond the reach of the man who set his eyes on it, while Wesley says they go swiftly, strongly and irrecoverably.
6:
The man with an evil eye is a host, and the warning is about his invitation. Matthew Henry notices that both classes already warned are exposed here, the man given to appetite being glad of good cheer and the man who saves at home glad of a dinner at another man’s table; neither should accept every invitation, nor thrust himself in uninvited. There are hosts, he says, with a fair tongue and an evil eye, who say what a host is expected to say and grudge their guests every bit; such a man loves his money too much and his friends too little to have any comfort of what he pays for, so that his feast is his own penance, and if he cannot bid his friends welcome he ought not to add the guilt of dissimulation by inviting them. Adam Clarke puts it shortly, never to eat with a stingy man, and adds that the guest will afterwards blame himself for accepting. Charles Ellicott calls the host sordid and grudging, one who calculates the cost of every morsel, reads the vomiting as disgust at hospitality not freely offered, and makes the lost sweet words the thanks spent on a cold welcome.

Keil and Delitzsch take the phrase about his thinking for a man reckoning with himself while he says eat and drink; the evil eye they define as the envy and selfishness of egoism, and they note that the Greek version refers the look to enchantment, the same words in several languages serving for eyeing, bewitching and envying. John Gill makes the line a rule of judgment, that a man is not what his mouth declares him but what his heart thinks, and John Wesley that he is judged by the constant temper of his mind rather than by his words.

Speaking in the ears of a fool is refused on the same principle. Keil and Delitzsch explain that the phrase means not whispering but speaking so as to be distinctly perceived, and that the fool is the heavy and dull man whose heart is covered as with grease against all impressions of better knowledge, so that he has no susceptibility for what the words intend but only contempt. Henry treats it as the rule against casting pearls before swine: some will jest at anything however prudently spoken, despising not only a wise man’s words but the wisdom in them, which is the very thing that might have edified them; such men forfeit good advice, and a wise man is advised to hold his peace and try whether the wisdom of that will be regarded. Gill says it is beating the air, and Ellicott that it is a waste of time to explain matters to a dull man.

The old landmark and the fields of the fatherless bring in the kinsman. Keil and Delitzsch observe that the proverb is made out of parts of two earlier ones, and give the verb the sense of unjustly invading another man’s ground; if orphans have no kinsman to buy back an inheritance that has passed into other hands, they have a mighty deliverer who will restore what they lost. Clarke sets out what the office covered, the right of the next in blood to redeem an alienated estate, avenge a murdered relative and marry a brother’s childless widow, and notes that the strength lies in the justness of the claim, the extent of his influence and the powerful abettors of such a cause; here, the orphans having no kinsman, God takes their cause himself, and his heaviest curse falls on those who rob an orphan. Henry adds that God counts himself affronted in the injuries done them, that his omnipotence is engaged for their protection, and that being children they do not even apprehend the wrong done them. Ellicott and Wesley keep the same office, a mighty deliverer where no kinsman is.
12:
Instruction and the rod are treated together. Matthew Henry reads the first verse as a parent persuading a child to give his mind to his book and his catechism and not think it enough to give them the hearing, since the heart is applied to instruction when instruction is applied to the heart. John Gill reads it as a call to bring the heart to the place of instruction, not the body only. Keil and Delitzsch observe that the admonition may be taken as offering discipline or as applying the heart to it, according as the divine origin or the human medium is accented, and that it is addressed alike to educators and educated.

On the correction, Henry allows that a tender parent can scarcely find in his heart to do it, but finds it necessary and dares not withhold it; the stripes being those of the sons of men, not such as we give to beasts, and the rod will not kill the child but keep him from the courses that would. Keil and Delitzsch settle the promise. It does not say the child will not fall under destruction, nor that the blow must not be one he dies of; it says he will not die of it, so that a father need only strike where the fault deserves it; the emphatic pronoun following means that the man who administers the correction is the man who saves the child. Charles Ellicott says a moderate correction will not injure him but quite the reverse, and reads the deliverance from hell as one from the abode of the dead, death being sin’s punishment and long life the reward of well-doing. John Wesley calls it a likely way to prevent his ruin, Gill insists the stripes be proportioned to the fault and to what the child can bear, and Adam Clarke notes that the correction of children was a favourite point of discipline with this writer.

Turning to the pupil, Keil and Delitzsch note that wisdom is inborn in no one, and support it with an Arab proverb that the wise man knows how the fool feels because he was once a fool himself; they add in a note the second half, that a fool does not know how a wise man feels because he has never been one, and record hearing it from a missionary in Constantinople. They observe that these words of the wise are penetrated by the subjectivity of an author, the father making his own heart the measure of the son’s progress. Ellicott and Gill explain the reins as the seat of the deepest affections, answering to the heart before.

The warning against envying sinners produces a grammatical dispute and a practical one. Keil and Delitzsch report that several versions make the second half an independent clause, be thou daily in the fear of the Lord, and object that one may speak of acting or walking in the fear of God but not of being in it, and that an elliptical reading would have required the verb. Henry gives the practical sense: do not grudge sinners their liberty or their success, since they are to be pitied rather than envied, their prosperity being their portion and indeed their poison; and he reports a reading by which the line forbids not envying but imitating them. The fear of the Lord, he says, is to be ours as our employment and as our element, a pleasure in contemplating God’s glory and complying with his will. Clarke reads the end promised as another life and the expectation as one of blessed immortality which shall not be cut off, quoting two old English versions; Ellicott makes it an end that shall be peace, Gill an end both of the prosperity of the wicked and of the afflictions of the righteous, and Wesley a happy end for those who fear God.
19:
The call to hear is put in a parent’s mouth, and Matthew Henry takes the passage as advice for parents to give their children. Hearing is at once evidence of wisdom and the means of more, since wisdom comes by hearing as faith does; we owe reverence to the fathers of our flesh, and much more to the Father of our spirits; and when the mother is grown old the children are commonly grown up, but not therefore past being taught. Charles Ellicott renders the opening as a charge to hear whatever others may do, and takes the way for the way of God, which John Wesley expands as ordering the whole course of one’s affections and actions. John Gill notes that hearing is the road to being wise unto salvation.

Adam Clarke pauses to survey the chapter, observing how much of it is given to eating and drinking: the pupil is directed on his conduct at the tables of the rich, on his dealings with the covetous, and on public entertainments, where riot and debauch were usual. He borrows from Calmet four reasons, the useless expense, the loss of time, the danger of bad company, and the risk of irregular habits and a voluptuous life. Gill allows wine in moderation but not among excessive drinkers, lest the habit be caught; Ellicott glosses the drowsiness as what follows such debauches; and Keil and Delitzsch render the last line as sleepiness clothing a man in rags.

Keil and Delitzsch then consider how this part of the book is put together. The verses about the father and mother can be read as independent couplets, they say, but the last leans back on the first in address and expression, so that the four form a whole; the compiler may have found two of them already made, while the first and last bear his own hand. The following verses they call a hexastich warning against unchastity, in which what earlier chapters set out at length is repeated in miniature pictures, and keep an older rendering in which wisdom herself asks for the heart.

The duty to parents draws a blunt remark from Clarke. The caution against despising a mother in her old age is very necessary, he says, since very old women are generally helpless and burdensome; but these circumstances do not lessen the child’s duty, which the divine command strengthens. Gill adds that a father who has lived longer has the larger experience.

Buying the truth is taken as a charge to pay any price. Clarke says the knowledge of God is to be acquired at all events, that no pains spent on it can be too much, and that once acquired no consideration should deprive a man of it, who should guard it even at the risk of his life; he quotes an old English version rendering the line as labouring to get the truth and not selling wisdom away. Wesley says the same, to purchase it on any terms and spare no cost. Ellicott observes that the truth here is described under three heads, wisdom and self-discipline and understanding, all to be had from God, who gives liberally and without price. Gill, having made the truth the whole body of Gospel doctrine, denies that the buying is of books, as one rabbi understood it; the Bible should be bought, but that does not reach the sense.

On the joy of a righteous man’s father Gill makes two restrictions: the rejoicing is over a son who is righteous and not rich, and it belongs to a father himself righteous, since wicked men are unconcerned about a son’s character so long as he thrives. He reads the next line as a wish rather than a promise, that a child should make his parents’ old age easy by ministering to their necessities, following their example and supporting religion to the utmost of his power.
26:
The request for the heart is taken by three voices as God’s, not a father’s. John Gill says these are not the words of a man to his son, since the claim to a heart belongs to God and not to a creature, and makes them the words of Wisdom; the heart of a wicked man is scarcely worth having, being possessed already by another, and the meaning is to give the heart neither to women nor to wine but to him who asks it. Adam Clarke makes it the speech of God to every human soul, and reduces the exhortation to three words, believe, love and obey, the sum, he says, of God’s counsels to every child of man. Charles Ellicott observes that the heart is the one gift worthy of acceptance and the only one God will accept, yet the very offering a man tries to keep back, putting in its place alms, unreal prayers and obedience in matters of little moment.

The warning against the strange woman is given in figures. Gill takes the deep ditch for insatiable appetite and collects two classical comparisons, one likening such a woman to the sea, which devours whatever it is given and shows nothing for it, and another naming her after the whirlpool that swallows all a man has; the ditch has no bottom, so that those who fall keep sinking till they reach the bottomless pit. On her lying in wait he reports an interpreter who reads a man of prey, and prefers himself a beast of prey, ravenous and never satisfied. Clarke states the case in a sentence, that more iniquity springs from this one source than from any other cause in the whole system of sin, and that women and strong drink cause many millions to transgress. Ellicott explains the multiplying of the faithless by calling the vice a fruitful source of faithlessness towards man and God alike.

Keil and Delitzsch mark the transition to drunkenness and account for it: the two sins are nearly related, since drunkenness excites fleshly lust, and a man made in the image of God must first brutalize himself with drink before he can wallow with any delight in the mire of sensuality. They note that the poem which follows outgrows the couplet form of the rest and becomes an ode, and render its opening as questions asking whose is the woe, the grief, the contentions, the wounds without cause and the dimness of eyes.

On those questions Clarke offers a physiological reading. He takes the first two interjections not as words at all but as the natural sounds men make in drink, from illness or from the nauseating effect of too much liquor; the contentions and babblings are over subjects the drinkers neither understand nor are fit to discuss, the wounds come of falling out about nothing, and the red eyes are either bloodshot with drink or blackened in a fight. All these, he says, mark out the men who sit long at wine as clearly as any description could. Ellicott glosses the wounds as those that might have been avoided and serve no good end, and would render the last question as dimness rather than redness of eyes. Matthew Henry, treating the passage as fair warning against drunkenness, adds the counsel with it: red wine was accounted the best and is called the blood of the grape, and some wine looks so well that it seems to say come and drink me, moving itself aright and going down smoothly; but a man is to be ruled by reason and religion rather than by sense, and must not let the heart walk after the eye, which is a deceitful guide. Those who would be kept from any sin, he says, must keep themselves from all its occasions and beginnings, and be afraid of coming within reach of its allurements.
30:
The mixed wine is explained first. Charles Ellicott says the verb means to test, to see whether the wine suits the drinker, and adds that ancient wines were not drunk pure but diluted with water or spiced; John Wesley gives both, water or ingredients to make it strong and delicious. John Gill describes the men who will not stir from it, spending whole days and nights over it.

On the counsel not to look at the wine, Gill would render it because it is red, notes that red was the most esteemed colour there, and says it is not unlawful to look at the colour and judge a wine by it; what is forbidden is the greedy eye that raises a vehement desire, as looking on a woman to lust after her. Adam Clarke makes it personal: however good the wine, it will be a snare to a man addicted to it who has no self-command. Ellicott renders the two clauses as sparkling and as gliding easily down the throat, and Wesley that the wine seems to smile upon a man.

The serpent produces the chapter’s one piece of close grammar. Keil and Delitzsch ask whether the words for its end are the subject, as two old versions and one scholar take them, making the verbs attributive; they answer that the end of the wine is not like a serpent but like the bite of one, and that the wine itself, apart from its consequences, is the serpent. The word might be read adverbially, after an old Latin rendering, but the author could have written it so plainly had he meant it; they settle on a substantival clause: its end is, like a serpent it biteth. Gill supplies the consequences without the grammar: it goes down sweetly and leaves a sting, nausea and giddiness, weakness of the eyes, trembling in the limbs, palsy and gout, and sharp reflections in an awakened conscience.

The strange things the drunkard sees are read two ways. Gill offers first other men’s wives, since excess of wine leads to whoredom, then a rendering by which the word means strange things, so that a man sees double and imagines that trees walk. Ellicott gives the same alternatives, impurity as the attendant of drunkenness or the fantastic visions of a disordered brain, and glosses the perverse things as notions of right and wrong distorted. Clarke answers the verse with six lines of Herbert on the drunkard who has lost the reins, is outlawed by himself, and forfeits his manhood with every right that is not a beast’s.

The man lying in the midst of the sea is an image of insensibility. Gill keeps it to a ship, in which a drunken man reels as the vessel does. Clarke draws the picture out: the man is regardless of life, like one who climbs the shrouds while drunk, clasps the mast-head and falls asleep there, whence he must shortly fall to the deck and be dashed to pieces or into the sea and be drowned; and he turns to the reader with the chapter’s own figure of a knife at the throat. Ellicott offers both that the sleeper would be drowned for trusting a smooth glassy surface and that a roll of the ship might hurl the other man into the waves, adding that the verse may mean the ground under a drunken man seems to rock. On the last verse Gill and Wesley report his own words, that he felt no pain and needs only sleep before returning to his course; Ellicott says he longs to rouse himself so as to go back to his debauch; and Clarke closes by observing that after all this disgrace the man proposes to repeat it, and that sin makes a man contemptible in life, miserable in death and wretched for ever, so that it is strange men should love it.
